children: With internal job posting participation up over 200 per cent and women's participation up seven-fold, the CHRO explains how transparent career pathways and AI capability building are preparing a multi-employer airport workforce for expansion

At Bangalore International Airport Limited (BIAL), the workforce is being asked to absorb two large changes together: a bigger airport and a more AI-driven way of running it. Real-time AI now supports passenger flow, cargo and operations, and the people behind them include security staff, ground handlers, cargo teams and data scientists, employed by multiple organisations on one campus.

Nalini George, chief human resources officer (CHRO) at BIAL, who spent six years building talent strategy at Rakuten before moving into airport operations, treats the two as a single people agenda. In this conversation, she explains how frontline hiring is shifting towards digital fluency and adaptability, why BIAL keeps one consistent message on AI and jobs, and how a competency-based career framework has lifted internal job posting participation by over 200 per cent, with women's participation growing seven-fold.

BIAL is building itself into what the industry is calling an "algorithmic airport," running real-time AI across passenger flow, cargo and operations. Two years into the CHRO role, what has that shift changed about the skills you're hiring for on the frontline compared to what you inherited in 2024?

The shift to becoming an algorithmic airport has fundamentally changed how we think about talent. While operational excellence remains non-negotiable in a safety-critical environment, we are increasingly hiring for digital fluency, adaptability, and data-driven decision-making alongside traditional operational capabilities.

In the past, many frontline roles were primarily focused on process execution, compliance, and operational discipline. Today, those same roles require employees to work confidently with AI-powered systems, real-time operational dashboards, predictive insights, and intelligent automation that support everything from passenger flow and cargo movement to airport operations.

As a result, we place greater emphasis on individuals who are comfortable using technology, interpreting data, solving problems, and making decisions in dynamic environments. We are looking for people who can combine operational expertise with curiosity, learning agility, and the ability to adapt to rapidly changing ways of working.

What has been particularly striking is that the defining skill for the future is not coding, but adaptability. Technology will continue to evolve, but the ability to learn, unlearn, and relearn quickly will remain invaluable. That is why we have invested significantly in building AI and digital capabilities across our workforce, ensuring that technology adoption becomes part of everyday work rather than the domain of specialists alone.

In simple terms, we have evolved from hiring primarily for operational excellence to hiring for operational excellence combined with digital intelligence, continuous learning, and future readiness. The airports of the future will be powered by technology, but their success will ultimately depend on people who know how to harness it.

An airport workforce spans security staff, ground handlers, cargo teams and data scientists under one roof, groups that experience AI very differently day to day. How do you calibrate one message on AI and job security across a diverse workforce?

One of the most important lessons we have learned is that you cannot have a one-size-fits-all conversation about AI in an airport ecosystem. A security officer, a ground handler, a cargo professional, and a data scientist will experience AI very differently in their day-to-day work. What connects them, however, is a shared need to understand what AI means for their role and their future.

Our approach has been to keep one message consistent: AI is here to augment people, not replace them. The purpose of AI is to make work safer, simpler, faster, and more informed by taking over repetitive tasks and providing better insights, while leaving critical human judgment, expertise, empathy, and decision-making where they belong: with people.

At the same time, we recognise that the questions employees have are deeply personal. People are not asking whether AI will change work. They already know it will. What they want to know is, "What does this mean for me?" That is where transparency becomes critical. We have found that uncertainty creates anxiety, but understanding creates confidence.

That is why our focus has been as much on capability building as on technology deployment. We want every employee, regardless of role, to feel equipped to work alongside technology and confident about their ability to grow with it. The conversation is not about protecting jobs from AI. It is about preparing people for a future where technology becomes an increasingly powerful partner in their work.

Ultimately, airports will always be people businesses. Technology can help us move passengers more efficiently, improve safety, and make better decisions, but it is people who build trust, respond in moments of uncertainty, solve complex problems, and create memorable experiences. Our role as leaders is to ensure our employees see AI not as a threat to their future, but as a tool that helps them thrive in it.

You spent six years building talent strategy inside Rakuten, a business built natively around technology, before moving into a much older, more physical industry. What has that contrast taught you about how ready a traditional operations-heavy workforce is for AI, compared to a tech-native one?

Technology readiness and technology maturity are two very different things. One of the biggest lessons from moving from a technology-native company to an airport ecosystem is not to confuse proximity to technology with readiness for change.

At Rakuten, technology was native to the business. Employees lived and breathed digital innovation every day. At BIAL, the business is fundamentally operational and physical, but increasingly technology enabled. On the surface, those worlds appear very different. In reality, the people challenge is remarkably similar: how do you make technology meaningful for employees, build the right capabilities, and create a workforce that remains adaptable as the business evolves?

What I have found is that readiness for AI is less about the industry people work in and more about their mindset. Our frontline teams may not all be technologists, but they operate in an environment that demands constant adaptation. Every day, they respond to changing passenger volumes, operational complexities, safety requirements, and customer expectations. That adaptability is a powerful foundation for embracing new technologies.

The key is helping people see technology as a solution to real problems rather than technology for its own sake. Whether you are a security officer, a cargo specialist, an engineer, or a data scientist, people adopt new tools when they make work safer, simpler, faster, or more effective.

That is why our philosophy has remained consistent across environments: first fix the process, then use technology to make it better. AI is not a substitute for good processes or good people. It is an enabler that helps both perform at a higher level.

Ultimately, AI is not a technology strategy, it is a people strategy. The organisations that succeed will not necessarily be those with the most sophisticated algorithms, but those that create the confidence, capability, and culture needed for people to harness them. My experience across both technology and airport ecosystems has convinced me that when people are empowered to learn and adapt, industry becomes irrelevant. Human potential remains the greatest competitive advantage.

You've spoken about using data to guide career growth and using technology to challenge the status quo. What does that actually look like for someone in a ground operations role at BIAL, rather than a desk-based analyst, when you're mapping out their next skill path?
It starts with removing the idea that a career has to be a straight line.

For someone in ground operations, growth does not have to mean moving up within the same function. It could mean building deeper expertise, moving across functions, taking on new operational responsibilities, or progressing towards leadership. Programmes such as EXCEL (Our internal policy) help make those cross-functional opportunities more visible and accessible.

Our competency-based career framework shifts the conversation from “What is your current job?” to “What capabilities do you have, and what capabilities do you want to build?” That is important because the future of work will be shaped less by job titles and more by transferable skills.

Data helps us make that conversation practical. It allows us to identify capability gaps, understand emerging skill requirements, and create more personalized learning and career pathways. It also helps challenge traditional assumptions about who can move into which role and opens up opportunities that employees may not have previously considered.

The impact is already visible. We have seen Internal Job Posting participation increase over 200 per cent in the last few years, while women's participation has grown seven-fold, demonstrating that when opportunities become more transparent, people are far more willing to pursue them.

Ultimately, for an employee on the ground, career growth should not be limited by the function they started in. It should expand with the capabilities they build. Our role is to use data, technology, and development opportunities to create a career ecosystem where every employee can continuously learn, grow, and remain future-ready.

Your recent thinking on retention has centred on belonging over benefits. As AI automates more of the passenger and cargo experience, where does that sense of belonging get built for employees whose daily work is increasingly mediated by a screen or an algorithm rather than a person?

I have always believed that people stay because they feel they matter, not because they receive one more benefit. Benefits can support the employee’s experience, but belonging is what creates a lasting connection to an organisation.

As AI becomes more embedded in passenger services, cargo operations, and day-to-day decision-making, there is a natural concern that work could become more transactional or mediated by screens and algorithms. My view is exactly the opposite. The more technology advances, the more important the human experience becomes.

Belonging is not built through technology. It is built through purpose, growth, relationships, recognition, and the feeling that your contribution matters. AI can help employees work more efficiently, but it cannot replace the sense of pride someone feels when they solve a complex operational challenge, support a colleague during a critical moment, or contribute to creating a seamless experience for millions of passengers.

For us, the question is not how technology affects belonging, but how technology can create more space for it. If AI removes repetitive tasks, simplifies processes, or gives employees better information, it allows them to spend more time on the aspects of work that are uniquely human: collaboration, problem-solving, learning, innovation, and connection.

That is why we invest heavily in career growth, learning opportunities, leadership accessibility, cross-functional experiences, wellbeing, and community building. We want employees to see a future for themselves at BIAL and to feel connected not just to their role, but to a larger purpose and ecosystem.

Ultimately, belonging has never been about how much technology exists in the workplace. It is about whether people feel seen, valued, and connected to something meaningful. In fact, as work becomes more digital, that human connection becomes even more important. The future airport may be powered by algorithms, but it will continue to be sustained by people who feel a sense of purpose, pride, and belonging in what they do.

BIAL's expansion plans and its AI ambitions are both moving fast at the same time, across a workforce ecosystem of thousands of people spanning multiple employers on one campus. Which of the two is pulling harder on HR's bandwidth right now, and how are you sequencing between them?
I do not see them as competing priorities. In many ways, they are two sides of the same transformation.

Expansion creates scale. AI creates capability. To deliver a larger, more complex airport sustainably, we need both. The real challenge for HR is ensuring that growth and technology evolve together rather than on separate tracks.

As BIAL continues to expand, our focus is naturally on building leadership pipelines, strengthening critical capabilities, attracting talent, and creating career opportunities across the airport ecosystem. At the same time, AI is changing how work gets done, how decisions are made, and what skills will be most valuable in the future. If we focused only on growth, we would risk building yesterday's workforce for tomorrow's airport. If we focused only on AI, we would risk losing sight of the people and capabilities required to operate at scale.

So, our approach has been to sequence them together. Every conversation about workforce growth includes a conversation about future skills. Every discussion on technology adoption includes a discussion on capability building, leadership readiness, and employee experience.

This becomes particularly important because BIAL is not transforming a workforce within a single company. We are part of an airport ecosystem where tens of thousands of people across multiple employers contribute to the passenger experience every day. As that ecosystem grows and becomes more technology-enabled, our responsibility is to ensure that the experience evolves without losing the sense of place and human connection that underpin our Feels Like BLR philosophy, bringing together people, culture and thoughtful details to create an experience rooted in our cultural identity.

Ultimately, if I had to choose where HR is investing the most energy, it is not in expansion or AI individually. It is in ensuring that people can thrive in a future where both are happening simultaneously. The question is no longer whether the airport will grow or whether technology will advance. Both are certain. The real differentiator will be how effectively we help people adapt, grow, and succeed as those changes unfold.
Savi Khanna
BW Reporters Assistant Editor, BW Businessworld
